## {.center}

::: {.big}
A Methods sentence is not an analysis rule.
:::

**Someone has to decide what it means. That someone is you.**

Today: one published paper, one public dataset, and every decision in between.

::: {.notes}
(1 min) Timing: about 50 minutes for the 17 main slides, leaving the appendix for questions
or for students to read later. Open cold on this sentence - do not introduce NHANES yet.
The whole first act is designed so students feel the problem before meeting any vocabulary.
:::

## Start with four words from the Methods

> "The study inclusion criteria were participants **aged >18 years** with evidence of
> MASLD."
>
> — Kueh et al., *BMJ Open* 2026

**Before you write any code: who exactly qualifies?**

- `>18` means **19 and older**
- `≥18` means **18 and older**

There is no third reading. One of them is what the authors did, and the paper does not
tell you which.

::: {.notes}
(3 min) Put the question to the room and wait. Most will say "obviously they meant 18 and
over" - that is the instinct to interrogate, not to trust. Do not reveal the counts yet.
:::

## One character moves 70 people

::: {.big}
70 participants are exactly 18
:::

| Age rule | Final N | Deaths |
|---|---:|---:|
| **Published paper** | 6,300 | 585 |
| Our reproduction, `≥ 18` | 6,371 | 586 |
| Our reproduction, `> 18` | **6,301** | **585** |

The strict reading — the one the paper literally prints — lands one row from the published
N and reproduces the death count exactly.

::: {.notes}
(4 min) Let the table land before commenting. The lesson is not "use > 18". It is that a
question you could have waved away is worth 70 people and was answerable in one line of
code. Ask: how would you have found this if you had not been looking for it?
:::

## But the evidence does not settle it

| Evidence | Points to |
|---|---|
| The printed Methods text says `>18` | **`> 18`** |
| N = 6,301 and 585 deaths vs published 6,300 / 585 | **`> 18`** |
| Published mean age 51.0 (SD 16.6); ours is 51.0 (16.6) under `≥18`, 51.4 (16.3) under `>18` | **`≥ 18`** |

**So we cannot resolve it — and saying so is the finding.**

Report the ambiguity, show both, and let the reader see what turns on it. Typography is
evidence of what was printed, not proof of what was intended.

::: {.notes}
(4 min) This is the most valuable slide in the deck, because the answer is genuinely
unresolved. Students expect exercises to have answers. Real reproduction produces
documented uncertainty, and a defensible "we could not tell, here is both" is a stronger
result than a confident guess.
:::

## That was the whole method

::: {.ppdc}
**Paper** — what does the article actually say?

**Problem** — what is ambiguous, missing, or unmeasurable in the data?

**Decision** — what rule did we implement, and why?

**Consequence** — who entered or left, and what *kind* of change was it?
:::

Every decision gets one of three marks:

| | |
|---|---|
| **✓** | direct translation — the paper determines the answer |
| **◆** | judgment call — the paper leaves it open, we chose |
| **⚠** | unresolved conflict — the evidence disagrees with itself |

::: {.notes}
(3 min) Keep this framework on the board for the rest of the session. Students should be
able to produce these four lines for any step of their own paper by P1. The three marks
matter because they license different sentences in a write-up: a judgment call needs a
rationale, an unresolved conflict needs a sensitivity analysis.
:::

## What NHANES is, in one slide

**Cycle** — one two-year survey wave. We use six: 2007–08 through 2017–18.

**Component** — a topic file inside a cycle: demographics, body measurements, blood
pressure, laboratory panels, questionnaires.

**Variable** — a column inside a component: age, waist circumference, triglycerides.

**`SEQN`** — the participant ID that joins components for the same person.

::: {.callout-important}
NHANES is a **repeated cross-sectional survey**. Each cycle samples new people. Mortality
is added afterwards by linkage, which gives prospective follow-up — but never a second
measurement of anybody.
:::

::: {.notes}
(4 min) This is all the vocabulary needed for the next 40 minutes. Resist naming component
files - DEMO, BMX, TRIGLY mean nothing yet and the variable map exists for that. The
callout pre-empts the commonest misconception: students treat NHANES as a cohort study.
:::

## The journey: 59,842 people to 6,371

::: {.big}
59,842 → 36,580 → 6,371
:::

| | |
|---|---|
| **59,842** | everyone in six NHANES cycles |
| **36,580** | after age eligibility |
| **6,371** | after the disease definition, the exposure, and mortality linkage |

The paper reports **6,300**.

**Three numbers now. The reasons behind them are the next six slides — and the reasons
matter more than the arithmetic.**

::: {.notes}
(2 min) Deliberately withholding the step-by-step funnel. Novices cannot tell which of
eight rows matters; they can hold three numbers. The full typed funnel is in the appendix
and in COHORT_BUILD_STEPS.md for anyone reconstructing the work.
:::

## Not everything that leaves is missing data

Triglycerides are measured only in NHANES's **fasting laboratory subsample**, which
carries its own weight (`WTSAF2YR`).

| What happened | How many adults | What kind of loss |
|---|---:|---|
| Outside the fasting-weight frame | 21,618 | **design** |
| Inside it, but missing an input we need | 792 | **item missingness** |

::: {.callout-important}
**These need opposite responses.** A design restriction is answered by the right weight and
a sentence naming the population you are left with. Item nonresponse is answered by a
missing-data analysis. Adding them together and calling the total "attrition" is wrong
three ways at once.
:::

::: {.notes}
(5 min) The single most transferable epidemiologic idea in the deck, and the one this
audience already has machinery for. Be careful with the first row: "outside the
fasting-weight frame" is the defensible phrase. It is NOT the same as "never asked to
fast" - 2,031 adults carry a weight of exactly zero, and 819 have all four inputs with no
valid weight at all. See the appendix slide.
:::

## A code means what *its own* codebook says

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Triglycerides** (`LBXTR`)

`77` is a triglyceride of **77 mg/dL**.

A real measurement.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Drinks per drinking day** (`ALQ130`)

`777` means **refused**.
`999` means **don't know**.

Not measurements at all.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
Apply one global missing-value rule and you either delete valid laboratory values or
convert **9 refusals** into people drinking 777 drinks a day. There is no NHANES-wide
rule. The codebook for *that variable*, in *that cycle*, decides.
:::

::: {.notes}
(3 min) Nine misclassified refusals would not have changed this paper's conclusion. Say
that - and then say that "it did not matter this time" is not a method. They found it by
checking.
:::

## Defining the disease takes four measurements

**MASLD** = fatty liver + at least one cardiometabolic feature. No liver-imaging measure
spans all six cycles (2017–18 added elastography, the earlier five have none), so the
paper uses a **Fatty Liver Index** built from four routine measurements:

triglycerides · **BMI** · liver enzyme (GGT) · **waist circumference**

Threshold: FLI ≥ 60. That leaves **6,376** people with fatty liver.

::: {.callout-warning}
## ◆ Notice what just happened
The exposure in this study is **BMI crossed with waist-to-height ratio**. Two of the four
inputs to the *disease* definition are BMI and waist. **The disease definition and the
exposure share their ingredients** — keep that in mind for M1.
:::

::: {.notes}
(4 min) The circularity is the most important methodological thread in the whole paper,
and it is planted here rather than argued. The paper's own TyG-index sensitivity analysis
is its attempt to address it. Equation and units are in the appendix; nobody needs the
coefficients on a slide.
:::

## A criterion can sound decisive and do nothing

The paper requires fatty liver **plus at least one** of five cardiometabolic criteria.

::: {.big}
It excluded 2 people
:::

6,376 with fatty liver → **6,374** with MASLD.

**Why.** The first criterion is essentially "high BMI or high waist", and FLI is *built
from* BMI and waist — so selecting on FLI ≥ 60 heavily **enriches** the cohort for that
criterion. It does not guarantee it: **89** people here have FLI ≥ 60 with a BMI under 25,
and 42 fail criterion (i) outright.

> **Report a filter by its effect, not its definition.** "MASLD required at least one
> cardiometabolic criterion" sounds like work; here it removed two people.

::: {.notes}
(4 min) Students describe filters by their definitions; readers judge them by their
effect. Both sentences are true and only one is informative. This is also the circularity
from the previous slide showing up in a second place.
:::

## ⚠ A vague exclusion has to be made precise

> "Individuals with significant alcohol consumption — more than two drinks per day for
> men and more than one for women — were excluded."

**Problem.** NHANES has no "drinks per day" variable. It has *drinks per drinking day*
and, separately, *how often you drink*. Three drinks every Saturday is `ALQ130 = 3` —
but **0.4 drinks/day**.

**Decision.** Rebuild average intake as frequency × quantity. That flags **427 people**.

**Consequence.** Applying it takes us to **5,944** — *further* from the paper's 6,300 than
leaving it off (6,371). So we build it, ship it, log the setting, and do not apply it.

::: {.notes}
(4 min) Be explicit that we implemented the exclusion and chose not to run it - the flag
is computed and saved, and one line turns it on. "Implemented" and "applied" are different
things. Also be fair to the authors: the paper never publishes its operational coding, so
this is one plausible implementation disagreeing with their N, not proof they skipped it.
:::

## The exposure is a 2 × 2 you have to build

Obesity = BMI ≥ 30 (≥ 25 for Asian participants). High central adiposity = waist-to-height
ratio ≥ 0.6.

| | WHtR < 0.6 | WHtR ≥ 0.6 |
|---|---|---|
| **Obesity** | Group I — 391 | Group II — 4,585 |
| **No obesity** | Group III — 787 | Group IV — 608 |

::: {.callout-tip}
## ✓ How we know the construction is right
Our four group BMI medians are **30.9 / 35.2 / 27.6 / 28.8** — identical to all four
published values. That check is independent of the N disagreement, so it isolates the
group logic from everything else.
:::

::: {.notes}
(3 min) Teach the move, not the result: when one number disagrees, find a statistic that
tests only the piece you are worried about. The paper's own table headers contradict its
Methods on the BMI cut-point - appendix slide - and the medians settle it.
:::

## ⚠ The variable you need may not exist in every cycle

**Why we care.** Asian participants get a different BMI cut-point (25, not 30).

**Problem.** NHANES did not identify Asian participants separately until **2011–2012**.
For 2007–2010 they are inside a combined "other race" category.

**Decision.** Apply the Asian cut-point only where Asian ethnicity can actually be
identified — and say so.

**Consequence.** **At most 17** participants could be grouped differently. An upper bound,
not a count of known errors.

<small>Ethnicity variable: `RIDRETH3`, available 2011–2018 only</small>

::: {.notes}
(4 min) Note the shape: the consequence is a bound, because the data cannot produce a
point estimate of the error. Bounding an unmeasurable limitation is a perfectly publishable
move and much better than silence. Where the variable does exist the rule moves 121 of 250
Asian participants, so it is not a negligible rule - just an unapplicable one.
:::

## The outcome lives in a different dataset

NHANES measures the exposure. It does **not** record who died.

Mortality comes from **NCHS linked mortality files** — separate downloads, joined on
`SEQN`, giving vital status, cause category, and follow-up through **31 Dec 2019**.

**◆ Decision: when does the clock start?** We use time from the **examination**, because
that is when BMI, waist and the blood work were measured. The paper does not say which it
used.

::: {.callout-warning}
A one-column error when reading these fixed-width files corrupts every result **silently** —
every model still runs. Sanity-check the parsed values before trusting anything.
:::

::: {.notes}
(3 min) "Outcome ascertainment is an analytic decision, not a clerical merge." The clock
choice is a genuine judgment call the paper leaves open; ours moves mean follow-up by
about 0.07 years, so it is defensible either way - but it should be stated.
:::

## Most of it reproduces — that is not the interesting part

| | Reproduced | Published |
|---|---:|---:|
| Analytic N | 6,371 | 6,300 |
| Deaths | 586 | 585 |
| Group IV HR, unadjusted | 15.14 | 15.13 |
| Group IV HR, adjusted | 2.91 | 2.89 |

**The interesting part is what the numbers support.** Adjusted, Group III is 3.03 and
Group IV is 2.89, both against Group I.

> Both groups have higher adjusted mortality than Group I. **Whether Group IV is worse
> than Group III is a contrast the paper never reports** — and similar point estimates are
> not evidence of equivalence.

::: {.notes}
(4 min) The reproduction succeeds and the disagreement is about interpretation, not
arithmetic. That distinction - reproducible but over-claimed - is the M2 genre in one
slide. Do not let students leave thinking a successful replication endorses the paper's
conclusion.
:::

## What to take to P1

For every step of your own paper, write four lines:

::: {.ppdc}
**Paper** — the exact sentence · **Problem** — what it fails to determine ·
**Decision** — your rule and why · **Consequence** — the change, and its type
:::

Then label each consequence: **eligibility · design · item missingness · target
population · outcome ascertainment**.

::: {.callout-tip}
An unexplained exact match is worth less than a discrepancy you can account for. Aim for a
**defensible audit trail**, not a matching number.
:::

**Where things live:** these slides = the reasoning · `COHORT_BUILD_STEPS.md` = exactly
what we did · `VARIABLE_MAP.md` = where each variable lives · the `R/` scripts = proof.

::: {.notes}
(3 min) Close here. The three-layer sentence matters: students should know which document
answers which kind of question, so they stop trying to get implementation detail off a
slide.
:::

# Appendix {background-color="#f0f0f0"}

## Appendix — the full analytic funnel {.dense}

| Step | Criterion | N | Type |
|---|---|---:|---|
| 0 | All NHANES 2007–2018 records | 59,842 | — |
| 1 | Age ≥ 18 | 36,580 | eligibility |
| 2 | FLI computable | 14,989 | design + missingness, fused |
| 3 | Fatty liver (FLI ≥ 60) | 6,376 | target population |
| 4 | MASLD (≥ 1 cardiometabolic criterion) | 6,374 | target population |
| 5 | Phenotype group assignable | 6,374 | missingness |
| 6 | Mortality-eligible and linked | **6,371** | outcome ascertainment |
| 7 | Alcohol exclusion applied = FALSE | 6,371 | analysis setting |

## Appendix — the fasting-weight domain {.dense}

| Step | Criterion | N | Type |
|---|---|---:|---|
| 1 | Age ≥ 18 | 36,580 | eligibility |
| 2 | Positive `WTSAF2YR` | 14,962 | design restriction |
| 3 | FLI computable | 14,170 | item missingness |
| 4 | Fatty liver (FLI ≥ 60) | 6,052 | target population |
| 5 | MASLD | 6,050 | target population |
| 7 | Mortality-eligible and linked | **6,048** | outcome ascertainment |

**6,371 and 6,048 answer different questions.** The paper does not report using survey
weights, so 6,371 is what reproduces it; 6,048 is the only set on which a design-aware
estimate can be computed.

## Appendix — "outside the frame" ≠ "never asked to fast" {.dense}

A missing or zero `WTSAF2YR` conflates at least three different states:

| | Adults |
|---|---:|
| No positive fasting weight | 21,618 |
| …of whom carry a weight of **exactly 0** | 2,031 |
| …of whom have a triglyceride value anyway | 966 |
| …of whom have **all four** FLI inputs | 819 |

So the weight marks *the analysable fasting domain*. It does not certify who was or was
not asked to fast — 819 people have the fasting measurement and no usable weight.

## Appendix — the Fatty Liver Index

```
       exp(L)
FLI = -------- × 100
      1 + exp(L)

L = 0.953·ln(TG) + 0.139·BMI + 0.718·ln(GGT) + 0.053·waist − 15.745
```

| Input | NHANES variable | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| Triglycerides | `LBXTR` | mg/dL |
| BMI | `BMXBMI` | kg/m² |
| GGT | `LBXSGTSI` | U/L |
| Waist circumference | `BMXWAIST` | cm |

All four arrive in the units the equation expects, so nothing is converted. Steatosis:
**FLI ≥ 60**.

## Appendix — the five cardiometabolic criteria {.dense}

At least one must accompany fatty liver:

1. BMI ≥ 25, or waist > 94 cm (men) / > 80 cm (women)
2. Fasting glucose ≥ 5.6 mmol/L, HbA1c ≥ 5.7%, or antidiabetic treatment
3. Blood pressure ≥ 130/85 mm Hg, or antihypertensive treatment
4. Triglycerides ≥ 150 mg/dL, or lipid-lowering treatment
5. HDL ≤ 40 mg/dL (men) / < 50 mg/dL (women), or HDL-targeted treatment

**Glucose note.** 5.6 mmol/L is 100.9 mg/dL; we coded ≥ 100. 212 people sit in that gap,
and re-running MASLD at ≥ 100.9 changes **0** classifications.

**Criterion 5 note.** NHANES has no variable for HDL-targeted treatment, so that clause is
not implementable.

## Appendix — the decisions ledger {.dense}

| | Decision or limitation | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| ⚠ | Age `≥ 18` vs `> 18` | 70 people; evidence points both ways |
| ⚠ | Alcohol exclusion built but not applied | 427 people if switched on |
| ⚠ | `cv_death` in the saved file = heart + cerebrovascular | 185 events vs the paper's 158 (heart only) |
| ◆ | Asian cut-point only where ethnicity is identifiable | ≤ 17 grouped differently |
| ◆ | Full file (6,371) vs fasting-weight domain (6,048) | 323 records |
| ◆ | Follow-up clock from examination, not interview | mean 6.76 y vs 6.83 y |
| ◆ | Composite comorbidity definitions | 1–3 percentage-point gaps vs Table 1 |
| ◆ | No survey weights, matching what the paper reports | the design-aware estimate is P4 |
